I'm about to try some non-systemd operating systems.

I want to see how compatible they are with the software I typically install. I figure this can benifit more than just myself if I install other people's favorites and run them as well as put them through a proper ringer. Then I can report back with the pitfalls.

I'll be trying slackware, gentoo, freebsd, and possibly manjaro switched to no-systemd as a control.

Give me your typical softwares.
I'm about to install slackware, gentoo, and freebsd in one evening. What of your favorite software do you want me to test compatibility on?

Little more detail:

Slackware is installed from 64bit 14.1 install dvd
Gentoo is amd64 minimal installation cd
Freebsd is amd64 10.3 disk1
Manjaro is xfce 16.06.1 x86_64

Installed in VirtualBox on an Arch.

Notes so far:

Slackware is by far easier to install than Arch. The only snag in a Slackware installation is Slackware's default is to install all software, 7+gigs. Getting it to install less is a bit of a bitch. Once installed boots into command line by defualt like arch does. I'm not sure how to make it boot into the display manager automatically as systemctl is obviously not present and the init.d and rc*.d is very different than what I've seen on debian and arch. The important thing is that unlike arch startx works out of the box. Very nice.

Next set is to check if guest additions installs without hickup. It does. Needed reboot which others usually don't need.

Gimp and vim installed by default, vim as elvis. Htop also on by default

Now we get to the hell of it, slackware package management. This is very fragmented. Set up slackpkg by editing /etc/slackpkg/mirrors and running slackpgk update. slackpgk search virtualbox. Does not know what that is.

The reason for this fragmantation is that slackware takes the package management mindset of not tracking dependences across packages. Obviously other users disagree because who when deploying a system wants to find each dependency and so there is an army of package management solutions and even some with their own repositories it looks like. This is the unix philosophy though. Single tools that do one job, can be traded out for others and built on by third parties. I'm sure this works great once you fing your fav package manager.

I'm going to try a few of these different methods and report on them. Some of them are essencially just compiling. I could always install anything by going to linuxfromscratch.org and following directions but that feels like cheating because that wouldn't review the distro. Will report back.

I've been working with SalixOS, which is a direct derivative of Slackware. Same deal with out-of-the-box installation of everything (it seems) under the sun, but it boots to a GUI (XFCE). Not too bad, if you ask me.

Tip: don't use your main machine for this experiment.

So far slackware is looking good.

Ubuntu is easiest. If you have a 64-bit machine, pls try PCBSD. It looks good, but last time I was trying things, I couldn't make anything co-install with windows like I did back in the day, so I had to put together a machine out of old parts. It was 32 bit, and PCBSD won't work on 32-bit.

Now that I know to virtualize, I need to retry everything I suppose.

So dress codes drive company culture. Whether that culture is uptight, classic, business, casual, preppy, whatever - you'll find that between the lines of the dress code. Enforcement of the dress code would dictate that someone that is not following the dress code is swaying from company culture. While an exception from time to time may not be an issue to be 'overdressed' consistently dressing in business attire contradicts a casual corporate culture that is trying to promote the ideals of everyone 'dressing down'. (Ultimately, dress codes are the ideals of someone in the company and their belief of how that impacts perception, capacity, motivation, etc., etc.) So, a dress code is not a 'minimum standard' it is 'the standard' set forth by that organization. And, that last sentence is where I believe your perception and that of the OP are not aligned thus creating confusion; they failed to see your definition as 'minimum standard' vs their interpretation of 'the standard'.

The difference with a 'casual Friday' vs an every other day business attire type of work place is that the standard is 'business' and the Friday is a flexible exception for anyone that wants it and not the driving force of that culture. That company probably believes that the casual Friday is a motivator and/or reward to their employees in some fashion. So they're not going to care if you over dress on that day because that is not their standard. If company culture is strong, the majority will make every effort to follow the business and/or casual as outlined by that culture's dress code.

Also, I find that the OP in that thread is confused in the difference between dress code and PPE. PPE is bottom-line about safety. It trumps dress code. I'm not going to go into the engine room without my PPE even if I am following dress code in every other way - bring on the ear plugs (get rid of dangly earrings), reflective vests (I don't care how pretty that blouse is) and safe shoes (fuck the heels).
